There exists this repository for the Millenium Prize Problems https://github.com/lean-dojo/LeanMillenniumPrizeProblems.

We can theoretically port them, although I wonder if we should ask the authors (Robert Joseph and Alex Bishop) to do the port or if we should do it.

They could not model everything perfectly, so it might make sense to wait, on the other hand it also does not look like that there will be much more changes, as the last commit was 3 weeks ago. Or we just port the ones, which are sure.
I remember the statement of Navier Dtones being misformalized there. Do you know if tvis is fixed now?

Felix Pernegger said:

I remember the statement of Navier Dtones being misformalized there. Do you know if tvis is fixed now?

I think they fixed it, atleast it says so in this commit https://github.com/lean-dojo/LeanMillenniumPrizeProblems/commit/540da94826f70f3edf4d4fc66ce6cda20e903f61.
But we also already have a PR for Navier Stokes FC#1457, so that might be a millennium problem that we should not port (yet).
For Navier Stokes we definitely want to go with FC#1457 by @Tomas Skrivan
P vs NP we already have and for the other ones it is not quite clear to me how complete the formalisations at https://github.com/lean-dojo/LeanMillenniumPrizeProblems are.

I think for other problems (e.g. the Hodge Conjecture) it would be nice to do those in a way that maximises the amount of background material that can be later upstreamed to Mathlib (i.e. use this as an excuse to add some more cohomology theory to Mathlib!)
Can you maybe open a issue for the Hodge Conjecture with the required prerequisites or do you think that doesnt make much sense yet?
I think, given that we have the "Milestone", having issues for the other two would make sense: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/milestone/8
Yes, I will open the Yang-Mills one then, it is probably the furthest away from being able to formalize it.

https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/4007

A new formalization of the Navier Stokes Conjectures -- would love to get some eyeballs on it for review and I am highly receptive to comments on style, idioms, best practices -- coming at this as a n00b to lean, but decades of formal systems design with [001|Scade|VHDL]
Instead of opening a new PR, can you please review FC#1457 ?
hey re: FC#1457 -- I have looked at that -- totally different scope and approach ...
I don't see why we would merge your AI-generated PR when several Lean experts have already spent time making a concurrent PR
Your statement of authority (decades of formal systems design) feels misguided

Paul Charlton said:

hey re: FC#1457 -- I have looked at that -- totally different scope and approach ...

Can you point out what the different approach is how its scope is different and why you chose to go that route instead. What are the trade-offs/benefits? What is better in your approach that potentially could improve FC#1457?

@Yaël Dillies re your PR -- I like it in general, a few missing items -- I will add the comment on your PR

  • Aggregator missing. Fefferman p.2 l.10–12 frames the prize as "we ask for a proof of one of the following four statements." That disjunction is the prize statement; File 1 only states the four routes as parallel theorems and never asserts A ∨ B ∨ C ∨ D.
  • Errata not incorporated. Two-part erratum: (a) p(x+e_j,t)=p(x,t) added to eq. (8), (b) sign correction to eq. (12). On (a), the condition is captured by pressure_periodic (line 211) but the docstring attributes it to eq. (10), which is velocity periodicity — wrong source, erratum uncited. On (b), eq. (12) is not in the file at all, so the sign correction has nothing to land on; whether eq. (12) belongs in a prize-statement file is debatable, but the silence is currently undocumented.
  • t > 0 instead of t ≥ 0. Line 162 (momentum), 129 (Rn force decay), 143 (periodic force decay) — Fefferman uses the closed half-line throughout.

@Moritz Firsching Disclosure upfront: I'm a n00b to Lean and to PDE-sector formal math. My background is control systems and safety-critical formal methods, and when I approached the Navier–Stokes problem from that direction every one of my instincts turned out to be wrong. A lot of the explanatory prose in my file is me documenting the PDE-sector domain-specific language — ambient assumptions like Lebesgue vs Riemann integration under dx/dxdt, gauge conventions on pressure. For an expert in PDE that documentation is mostly redundant; for someone arriving from a different formalism tradition it's the price of admission. I left it in because pedagogically it's a good move and I'd have wanted it as a reader.
TL;DR. #1457 inherits many of its operators from Mathlib; mine implements div, (u·∇)u, Δu, ∇p directly from Fefferman's Fin-indexed notation and adds named-prior structure so a downstream proof can cite spec clauses by name. A separate fixture (not part of this submission) bundles all hypotheses and variables into a single ManifoldConfiguration so I can rapidly model and test ideas against the proof oracle.

Happy to expand on any of this.

AI disclosure: I use AI for research and DocString|narrative consistency, I find AI terrible at actual solving and writing, especially lean4

@Moritz Firsching the TLDR version about mine -- lots of pedagogy so that a reader does not need to be an expert in PDE/NS to understand it; and every variable and hypothesis in the paper explicitly named and strongly typed instead of just the naked "proof blocks" for each route.

I'm curious, why do you prefer mentioning the namespace everywhere? I find the formulas difficult to read. Also doesn't it get exhausting typing it everywhere?

For example

noncomputable def vectorLaplacian {n : ℕ}
    (u : NavierStokesMillennium.Space n → NavierStokesMillennium.Space n)
    (x : NavierStokesMillennium.Space n) : NavierStokesMillennium.Space n :=
  (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin n) ℝ).symm
    (fun i : Fin n =>
      ∑ j : Fin n,
        fderiv ℝ (fun y => fderiv ℝ (fun z => (u z) i) y
          (NavierStokesMillennium.e j)) x (NavierStokesMillennium.e j))

@Tomas Skrivan perhaps not needed, but my first foray into lean kept binding to sites inside of mathlib instead of stubs I wrote -- so I scoped everything explicitly -- and, no real burden typing keystrokes -- bound 1 hotkey and muscle memory takes over.

and, I now imagine -- if lean4 bound to another site, it was because the I/o type signatures matched which meant it was already proven by someone else. In decades of work with other compilers and system I never developed a trust of "implicit bindings" everywhere. The same thing bit me on forcing everything to "pointwise everywhere" and lean was binding to "a.e." proofs (from my sloppy typing in early forays)
